overall_interpretation: France has a long-running mismatch between government income and expenditure. Debt relative to the economy has nearly doubled since 2000, with conspicuous jumps around the financial crisis and pandemic and a renewed rise after 2023. Persistent deficits, including deficits before interest for more than two decades, make this more than a story about interest on inherited debt. France raises a large amount of revenue relative to GDP in the comparison shown, but spending exceeds it by an unusually large margin. The longer spending comparison suggests a shift toward old-age benefits and health within a roughly stable total GDP share, rather than a broad doubling of spending alongside the debt ratio. These pictures describe a fiscal problem but do not establish why it constitutes a crisis now.

charts.spontaneous_understanding: The debt burden relative to GDP has climbed in steps and has recently resumed rising after a partial retreat.
evidence: 60.5% in early 2000 becomes 119.0% in mid-2026, labeled EUR3.6 trillion.
65.5% at end-2007 rises to 84.1% at end-2009 across the financial-crisis shading.
98.2% at end-2019 becomes 114.9% at end-2020 across the pandemic shading.
109.5% at end-2023 is followed by a rise to the latest point.
uncertainty: The ratio alone cannot distinguish borrowing from changes in GDP.
Event shading establishes timing, not how much each event caused.
No source or actual-versus-forecast status is visible.

charts.spontaneous_understanding: Annual budgets have remained in deficit, and the recent deficits would persist even with interest excluded. Interest has risen recently but is not the whole gap.
evidence: Every black total tick is below zero from 1995 to 2025.
The last blue primary surplus is labeled 2001, +1.7.
Large total deficits are labeled -7.4 in 2009 and -8.9 in 2020.
2025 total deficit of 5.1 consists of interest 2.2 (EUR67bn) and deficit before interest 2.9.
Interest in 2020 is 1.3 (EUR30bn); 2024 total deficit is 5.8.
uncertainty: The surplus years require reading the black tick separately from the bottom of the gray bar; the legend explains this but it takes attention.
The chart does not explain why the primary balance turned negative or stayed there.
A deficit each year need not imply the debt-to-GDP ratio rises each year, as chart 1 itself shows.

charts.spontaneous_understanding: France stands out among these comparators for both high revenue and even higher spending, leaving the largest total and primary deficits shown.
evidence: France revenue 52.1 and spending 57.2% of GDP leave a 5.1 gap and -2.9 balance before interest.
The EU aggregate has 46.4 revenue, 49.5 spending, a 3.1 deficit and -1.2 before interest.
Italy has a 3.1 total deficit despite a +0.8 balance before interest; Spain is at 0.0 before interest.
uncertainty: The title saying France collects the most is supported only within the displayed comparison, not every country.
The axis begins at 40, explicitly disclosed.
Germany spending minus revenue appears to be 2.6 whereas the deficit column is 2.7; this could be rounding.
This snapshot does not establish tax capacity, waste, service quality, or a preferred remedy.

charts.spontaneous_understanding: Spending has changed composition much more than its overall GDP share. Health and old-age benefits expanded, while several other categories and interest shrank.
evidence: Total spending is 56.1% in 1995 and 57.3% in 2024.
Social protection rises from 22.0 to 23.7, including old age rising from 11.0 to 13.4.
General public services falls from 8.3 to 6.2, including debt interest falling from 3.6 to 2.0.
Education falls from 5.8 to 5.1 and defence from 2.5 to 1.9.
Footnote says health is separate from social protection and 2024 figures are provisional.
uncertainty: Only endpoints are shown, so total spending may have moved substantially in between.
A falling GDP share is not proof of a cut in nominal or real spending.
No demographic, service-volume, or price evidence is supplied to explain the category changes.
The comparison ends in 2024, earlier than the 2025 budget snapshot and 2026 debt endpoint.

unsupported_interpretations: An imminent default or loss of market access.
A causal claim that ageing, a particular government, or waste created the debt crisis.
That interest alone accounts for the deficit or the rise in debt.
That the government can solve the gap only by cutting spending or only by raising taxes.
That the crisis and pandemic account quantitatively for all the growth in debt.
readability_and_missing_content: All four chart images and their labels were readable. No underlying sources, prose, forecasts methodology, market indicators, revenue history, or causal decomposition were available in this stage.
